core.text: Every Latin noun belongs to one of three groups, and the group never changes: this is its **gender (masculine, feminine or neuter, fixed for each noun)**, *genus*. It has little to do with real sex. *Fēmina* (woman) is feminine and *vir* (man) masculine, as you would expect; but *īnsula* (island) is feminine, *fluvius* (river) masculine and *oppidum* (town) neuter, purely because of their endings. Gender matters because every adjective and pointing word must match it.
English keeps gender only in *he / she / it*, and a river is *it*. Latin sorts nouns for things into the three groups too, so its *he*-words include rivers and its *she*-words tables.
Nouns in -a are feminine, nouns in -us (and -r) masculine, nouns in -um neuter. For any other ending, learn the gender with the word.

invented.la: Fluvius magnus est, īnsula parva est.
invented.en: The river is big, the island is small.

core.text: A noun's gender is fixed; an adjective's is not. *Rōmānus, Rōmāna, Rōmānum* is one adjective in three shapes waiting to match a noun: *vir Rōmānus*, *fēmina Rōmāna*, *oppidum Rōmānum*. The noun decides, the adjective follows. Do not read *Rōmāna* as 'a Roman woman' unless a feminine noun is there or understood.

more.text: The learner's notes: 1st-declension a-nouns are almost always feminine, 2nd-declension us-nouns (with the -r and -er kind) almost always masculine, um-nouns always neuter. Third-declension nouns are split fairly evenly among the three, so their gender is learned with the word: *pānis* m (bread), *carō, carnis* f (meat), *mare, maris* n (sea). A few nouns have an irregular gender that must simply be remembered: *propheta* m (prophet), *domus* f (house). A dictionary letter *c* means common gender: either masculine or feminine (*canis*, dog).

Ørberg cap. II: masculīnum -us (-r), fēminīnum -a, neutrum -um. Allen & Greenough add the rules of meaning that override the ending: names of males, rivers, winds and months are masculine; names of females, countries, towns, islands and trees are feminine (*Rōma*, *Corsica*, but also *Aegyptus* f). Neuter nouns always have the same form for subject and object, and their plural always ends in -a (A&G §31–35).
